title: Shared ownership
text: Pattern three: shared ownership on the hot path. Each message hands an order to a chain of handlers: on message, risk, route and publish. Who owns the order, and what does that ownership cost per message?

title: The general version
text: Ask for safe ownership with no latency budget, and you typically get std::shared_ptr, passed by value into every handler. Any handler could keep the order alive, nothing frees it early, and nothing dangles. It is correct and defensive. But every copy of a shared_ptr changes a reference count.

title: What a copy costs
text: The count lives in a control block, next to the order. Copying the pointer increments it; destroying the copy decrements it. Four handlers by value means four copies and four destructions: eight read-modify-writes per message. Once the program has started any thread, and every trading system has, libstdc++ makes them atomic: a lock-prefixed add. On this VM, a chain of those took about 16 nanoseconds each, against under one for a plain add. A locked instruction is also a full barrier, so later loads wait for it. And the handler chain compiled to 237 instructions, versus 29.

title: The hot-path version
text: The hot-path version decides ownership once. Orders live in a pool, created at startup, and owned by one object for the whole session. The message carries an index, and each handler borrows a plain reference. No counts, no atomics, no control block. Lifetime becomes a design rule: nothing on the hot path frees an order, and a slot is reused only when its order is done.

title: Measured
text: Measured on a shared cloud VM, pinned to one core: two million messages over a thousand orders, all in cache. With a thread started, shared_ptr by value took 72 nanoseconds per message, back to back. The pool with references took 5. One message at a time, the median was 107 versus 28, both including the timer. In a process that never starts a thread, libstdc++ skips the atomics, and by value took 17: still three times the pool. Passing the shared_ptr by const reference took 5.9. Almost all of the cost was the copies.

title: When shared_ptr is fine
text: shared_ptr is the right tool when lifetime really is shared and unpredictable: across threads, in callbacks and caches, and anywhere off the hot path. On the hot path, decide who owns the object, and lend references. Put that in the prompt: one owner, no reference counting per message. Then measure. The rule: own once, borrow everywhere, and never copy a shared_ptr per message.
